brief_description: A second PROTEST compared the MDS face spaces for White faces derived from Black versus White perceivers to evaluate cross-race agreement in perceived similarity structure. paper_value:
Based on the similarity ratings given by each racial group for each face set, we derived perceptual spaces using ordinal (nonmetric) MDS. In these spaces, Euclidean distances between faces represent perceived similarity. That is, faces perceived as more similar are spatially located closer together, while faces perceived as less similar are spatially located further apart.

The dimensionality of the face spaces was set to 6. This value was determined by evaluating lack of fit as a function of increasing dimensionality and by drawing on prior research that used similarity ratings to derive face spaces (e.g., Busey, 1998 ; Byatt & Rhodes, 2004; see Appendix B for details). In an ordinal MDS face space, the relative distance between faces reflects relative perceived similarities. All other aspects of the face space—namely, scale, rotation, and origin—can be changed without affecting relative distances, and are not in any way constrained by the observed similarity ratings. Therefore, to compare two different perceptual spaces, we must first bring the two spaces into alignment. We aligned the two spaces via a Procrustes transformation by scaling, rotating, and translating the face space of White perceivers to minimize the sum of squared distances of the location of each face to its associated location in the face space of Black perceivers.

To formally examine the role of race in discrimination ability, we employed a logistic regression model. Due to small age differences among participant samples and the established in ﬂuence of age on face recognition memory ( Fraundorf et al., 2019 ), we included age as a covariate. Thus, the predictors in the model included perceiver race, face race, the interaction between perceiver race and face race, and perceiver age ( z-transformed).
We found a signiﬁcant interaction between perceiver race and face race (eβ = 1.72, 95% CI [1.25, 2.38], z = 3.33, p < .001), indicating a cross-race effect. That is, the effect of face race on accuracy depended on perceiver race. White perceivers were better at distin-guishing between faces of White individuals than Black individuals (eβ = 1.67, 95% CI [1.33, 2.09], z = 4.47, p < .001), indicating that the odds of correct discrimination for White faces was 1.67 times that of Black faces. On the other hand, results for Black perceivers were consistent with little or no difference in the ability to distinguish same-race and cross-race faces ( eβ = 1.03, 95% CI [0.82, 1.30], z = 0.27, p = .789). Finally, the model indicated about a 14% drop in discrimination accuracy when age increased by 1 standard deviation (eβ = 0.86, 95% CI [0.80, 0.93], z = −3.70, p < .001).
